hook: Peter G. Neumann was a computer scientist who spent almost 70 years studying how computer systems fail and arguing that security must be designed in from the start, not patched on afterwards. He designed the file system of Multics at Bell Labs, led the Provably Secure Operating System project at SRI International, founded and edited the ACM RISKS Forum for 41 years, and from 2010 was SRI's principal investigator on CHERI, the hardware memory safety design that The New York Times reported is being adopted by companies such as Google and Microsoft. He was still working on it full time when he died on 17 May 2026, aged 93, from complications of a recent fall.

standing.standing: Peter G. Neumann stands as a foundational figure in computer security, with a career spanning almost 70 years. He designed the file system of Multics at Bell Labs and led the Provably Secure Operating System project at SRI International. From 2010, he was SRI's principal investigator on CHERI, a hardware memory safety design that The New York Times reported is being adopted by companies such as Google and Microsoft. He founded and edited the ACM RISKS Forum for 41 years, stepping down in April 2026. He was still working on CHERI full time when he died on 17 May 2026, aged 93.

quick_facts: Born 21 September 1932 in New York City; died 17 May 2026 in Santa Clara, California, aged 93
Studied mathematics at Harvard and earned a Ph.D. in applied mathematics and science there in 1961; Fulbright scholar in Germany, 1958 to 1960
Worked at Bell Labs from 1960 to 1970 and at SRI International from 1971, five decades as a principal scientist
Founded the ACM RISKS Forum and moderated it for 41 years, stepping down in April 2026
Founding editor of ACM Software Engineering Notes and founder of ACM SIGSOFT; Fellow of the ACM, IEEE and AAAS
As a Harvard sophomore in November 1952 he spent two hours at breakfast with Albert Einstein, arranged by his mother, who had made a mosaic portrait of the physicist
Annotated all 3,195 issues of the RISKS Forum, which built a following of hundreds of thousands of readers
Played bassoon, French horn, trombone and piano, and often led colleagues in Gilbert and Sullivan songs at conferences
Survived by his daughter, Helen Neumann
achievements: Designed the Multics file system, with hierarchical directories, access control lists and dynamically paged virtual memory segments, and helped design its input and output system
Led work on the Provably Secure Operating System (PSOS), which showed that security could be built into a system's design rather than retrofitted
Helped develop IDES, an early intrusion detection expert system, with Dorothy E. Denning in the 1980s

SRI International principal investigator on CHERI from 2010, the hardware capability architecture that brings memory protection to C and C++ and is now being commercialised through an international nonprofit alliance
Wrote Computer-Related Risks (1995), a case-driven guide to how computer systems fail and why
Advocated for transparency, verifiability and accountability in electronic voting systems

Was one of the first programmers with solo access to a stored-program computer, taking charge of Harvard's Mark IV every Friday evening from 1954, and co-wrote a paper with Frederick P. Brooks Jr. and others on using it to compose music
Was a key researcher on Emerald, a DARPA-funded 1990s project on detecting intruders in large networks, whose technology SRI later defended in patent lawsuits
Gave 4 million dollars anonymously to the San Francisco Symphony in December 2024 to save its chorus, his daughter said
